paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Roxanna is asking: why is *bodhichitta* necessary to reach omniscience?

We talk about practitioners on the lower paths, practitioners who don’t have *bodhichitta*. They have a deep understanding of emptiness. You can get pretty far along. You can become an arhat. You can get to a place where you never get upset again.
Translators, am I okay speed-wise?

You can get to that place, but you still have obstacles to omniscience. We always say, “Don’t waste your time getting to nirvana without *bodhichitta*,” because you have to do it anyway to get to the highest goals.
But why do you need *bodhichitta*?
I’m going to say it in an indirect way, and then you can think about it.

One of the things we say in Buddhism is that you shouldn’t speak badly of other people’s systems. You shouldn’t criticize other religions, systems of thinking, or belief systems. It’s quite a serious offense. It’s quite a serious vow later on, not to criticize other systems.
Why?

Imagine someone sitting here who has a belief system different than mine. I’ll use a really off-the-wall example just for fun. Someone believes in all of the Greek gods. They believe there are gods living up on a mountain controlling everything that happens: Zeus, Hera, Aphrodite, Apollo, all these gods on Mount Olympus.
I’m sitting here, and in my mind I’m kind of rolling my eyes: “Yeah, whatever. You believe there are a bunch of gods up there doing their thing.”
What am I doing when I do that?

This is how that person sees the world. Their seeds are opening, arising as them. Think about the Mind Only School. The subject and object come from the same seed. The person and the outside come from the same seed. Their seed is opening: their thoughts, the books they’ve read, the family they grew up in, the choices they’ve made—one seed after another opening.
They see themselves and they see their world in that way. They see their world in a way where there are Zeus and Apollo in the sky on Mount Olympus.
If I’m sitting there thinking, “Whatever, crazy talk,” what am I doing? I’m denying their experience. I’m denying their perspective on the world.
Then what am I subtly doing? I’m creating a seed to block knowledge. I’m cutting off a certain viewpoint, a certain possibility of existence.
What does omniscience mean? Omni. O-M-N-I. What does that root mean?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: All.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: It means all. Omni-science: all knowledge.

If I disparage the way someone’s seeds are opening to see the world, and I reject it—I didn’t say I accept it as true, but if I reject the way they see the world, then I’m rejecting a part of knowledge, a part of experience.
Therefore, I’m blocking my ability to have omniscience. What is omniscience? The ability to see all things: past, present, future, all perspectives of all people, all times, all beings.
If all perspectives are possible and I’m blocking that, I’m doing something that gets in the way of having that knowledge. I’m not saying whether it’s true or not. That’s not relevant.
Is it helpful for somebody? Does it help them? Does that way of seeing the world inspire them, make them a better person? Could it be a Lam Rim, a path toward understanding emptiness? Maybe.
That’s the connection of *bodhichitta* to omniscience, if I think about it.

chapters.title: Mind Only School and Upper Middle Way

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Luca is having an experience where she’s feeling very connected with others, and she’s feeling like she’s growing her capacity to do the exchanging-self-with-others practice. However, another seed is ripening for Luca, and she also feels like this is all just in her head. Christina is asking a similar question: is there anything out there? How do we think about this?
The answer is going to depend on what school we’re in.

In the Mind Only School, we’ve been spending a lot of time in the Words & Text class. It’s difficult. The Mind Only School says you’re not looking at outer objects. You’re looking at the ripening of the seeds in your mind.

We’ve been talking a lot about the refrigerator. The storage, the *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`], the foundation consciousness, stores the seeds. They say it’s right here in the heart chakra, very small. The seeds ripen in the *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`], and your mind sees that. You perceive it as an outer object, but what you’re looking at is in your mind, in the *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`].

We have this whole discussion: are the seeds the *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`] or are they not the *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`]? Are the seeds the refrigerator or are they not the refrigerator? The whole debate goes like that in this class. I think it’s very deep, and it can help you get very close to seeing how seeds write that. There’s no “actually,” but anyway.

Imagine you’re in a movie theater. You’re in that room. The seeds are ripening, and you’re looking at the screen. The projector is throwing the seed onto that screen: twenty-four frames a second in a movie theater, sixty-five in Buddhist philosophy. You’re looking at the walls of the movie theater. That’s all you’re ever looking at, says the Mind Only School.

There’s a big question that arises for most people in the Diamond Cutter Sutra courses. In the Mind Only School, the seeds are stored in the *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`], inside your heart. That’s easy to handle. “Where are my seeds? They’re in my heart chakra, in my *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`].” Small place, gazillion billion zillion seeds hanging out there.
Then what happens when you study the Diamond Cutter Sutra? At the very end of that course, there’s a question: according to the Upper Middle Way, where are the seeds stored?
Everyone’s mind blows up. It’s like the frog in the well that goes and sees the ocean.

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: They’re not stored, though, Tim. They are created every instant as we go through.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: In that question, in the course on the Diamond Cutter Sutra, the seeds are stored in your projections, in the projections themselves. Upper Middle Way says the seeds are stored in the projections themselves, in the names and labels and things that you toss out of your seeds all the time, that you can’t control.
You have to understand there’s no “in.” There’s no place. It’s not like in your *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`]. We use the word “in” to understand something because we use language.
Here Katrin said, “Where are they stored? In me.” Roxanna said, “In I.” Octavian said, “In the concept of me.”

Here’s my answer to your question. Imagine that movie theater is not only in your mind. The movie theater of the Mind Only School: seeds ripening on the walls of the *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`]. Imagine the world you’re perceiving right now is the movie theater.

If you have eyes and you’re not blind—I would really love to meet a deep Buddhist practitioner who doesn’t see very well or can’t see, because we always talk about eyes and mental images. I would love to discuss this.

If you have eyes and you’re looking around, imagine everything you’re looking at is the movie theater. It’s outside. Yes, it is outside. Yes, it’s there. But imagine the outside is the movie theater, always.
So go from the Mind Only School, which is in the *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`], and go outwards. Everything you’re experiencing is like the walls of the *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`].

Has anyone watched Star Trek? In Star Trek: The Next Generation and onwards, they have a thing called the holodeck. The door opens, you walk in, and the walls are gray with colored lines. You say, “Computer, start program.” It says, “What program would you like, Tim?” “I would like Sedona College of International Management office.” Then the room becomes this office.

In the Mind Only School, you’re inside. It’s in the mind. In the Upper Middle Way, it’s kind of like that, except it’s not just in your head, not only in your mind, though it’s helpful to think that way.

You’re looking, listening, feeling—whatever senses. We focus on the visual sense so much. Go spend a day blindfolded. You can do all the same analysis. If you’re a feeling-type person, the way you describe your inner landscape might be through feeling. You might not visualize things. You might feel pictures. Same thing.
When you’re interacting with the world, that’s the walls of the holodeck. But it’s out, and it’s outside.
So where are your seeds? That world you see is your seeds. The you in that world is the seeds.
What makes you a dog? It’s not that you’re a dog first and then you see a chew toy. You are a dog because it is a chew toy for you. You are Gina because of the world you see around you.
